items.title: New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010
items.desc: The new EU Bureaucracy Index measures the volume of EU law in force, and it shows a record high: At the end of 2025, the EU regulations and directives in force comprised around 47,600 standard pages, 118% more than in 2010. The volume of EU law has thus more than doubled in 15 years, and it continued to grow in 2025. The main drivers are sanctions regulations and new sets of rules in environmental, consumer and health law.

items.title: Queensland keeps learning disaster lessons. So why do we keep forgetting them?
items.desc: After an early start to Queensland's storm season, with severe storms and flooding already affecting communities across the state, attention is once again turning to disaster preparedness and response.

items.title: A star's 'obliquity' likely has little impact on a given planet's habitability
items.desc: A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumstellar disk that surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar-type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given star's initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

items.title: What draws data centers to a community?
items.desc: As Oklahoma communities weigh new data center development, research co-authored by a University of Oklahoma architecture professor offers insight into what draws major technology companies to locations—and why those choices matter locally.

items.title: Hurricane season wrap-up: El Niño fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic
items.desc: The 2026 hurricane season, which officially ends on Nov. 30, will be remembered as a year of contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic indication of a hurricane season influenced by a very strong El Niño. Below-normal activity across the Atlantic basin was offset by above-average activity in the Pacific, including two disasters in Hawaii.

items.title: Ultrathin 'rainbow' sails could power spacecraft and shade the Earth
items.desc: For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind "solar sailing," which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed feasible.

items.title: How alfalfa forms root nodules without rhizobia
items.desc: A research team led by professor Feng Jian at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology (IGDB) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has uncovered a cytokinin–NODULE INCEPTION (NIN) regulatory module associated with spontaneous root nodule formation in alfalfa (Medicago sativa).

items.title: New chemical route delivers first synthesis of plant compound with cough-suppressing potential
items.desc: Neotuberostemonine, a complex plant-derived alkaloid with promising antitussive activity, has remained a challenging target for chemical synthesis for nearly 30 years. Researchers have now achieved its first total synthesis, alongside the synthesis of neostenine and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. The findings also reveal how the nearly planar geometry of nitrogen atoms contributes to the oxidative instability of these alkaloids, offering new insights and synthetic strategies for natural-product chemistry and future drug discovery.

items.title: Quantum ingenuity can sidestep limits of conventional chips—while using commercially accessible components
items.desc: For decades, computers have steadily grown faster and more powerful. Avik Dutt, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Maryland, envisions another dramatic leap forward—one propelled by the quantum properties of light.

items.title: Laser light reveals where electrons accumulate in atomically thin semiconductor stacks
items.desc: Stacking semiconductors—the chips that power phones, computers and so much more—enables quicker signal movement with less energy, but how does the process actually work? Turns out shining a literal light on the semiconducting materials can help elucidate how the electrons move in the stack, according to a multi-institutional team in Japan. The approach could help inform the development of more efficient, low-power electronics, the researchers said.

items.title: Underwater robots reveal first salp species known to live exclusively in deep sea
items.desc: Salps are barrel-shaped gelatinous animals that play an important role in ocean ecosystems. More than 20 years ago, researchers observed an unfamiliar salp in the deep waters of Monterey Bay. Using specimens and data collected by MBARI's advanced underwater robots, Larry Madin, deputy director emeritus at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and an MBARI adjunct, recently published a detailed description of the glass salp (Vitreosalpa gemini) in the journal Marine Biodiversity. This striking species is the first salp known to live exclusively in the deep sea.

items.title: Myanmar earthquake reveals how fault history could help anticipate future slip
items.desc: Earthquakes are full of unknowns—scientists can't accurately predict exactly when or where the next big earthquake will strike. But some characteristics of 'the next big one' can be anticipated from what we know about a fault before it breaks, thanks to supercomputer simulations combined with an ever-increasing wealth of observational data.

items.title: New workflow advances programmable chromosome editing in plants
items.desc: A study published in Nature Protocols on Nov. 17 presents a detailed experimental workflow for programmable chromosome manipulation in plants. The platform was developed by a research group led by Gao Caixia at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

items.title: Catalysts come alive—electron microscopy reveals the secret dynamic life of nanoparticles
items.desc: University of Nottingham researchers have uncovered hidden nanoscale transformations that could help design cleaner fuels and more efficient catalysts.

items.title: Mitochondria rebranding: Goodbye, powerhouse of the cell. Hello, lungs of the cell?
items.desc: If you remember one thing from high school biology, there's a good chance it's this: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell.

items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
items.desc: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

items.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

items.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
items.desc: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

items.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
items.desc: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

items.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
items.desc: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

items.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
items.desc: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

items.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
items.desc: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

items.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
items.desc: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

items.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
items.desc: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

items.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
items.desc: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

items.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
items.desc: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

items.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
items.desc: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.desc: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.

items.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

items.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
items.desc: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

items.title: Holiday 2026 Reading List
items.desc: In the bi-weekly PS Book Recommendations newsletter —available for free to all registered PS readers—we highlight insightful, informative, or otherwise compelling books, written or recommended by PS contributors. Here, we present a selection of recent works by PS contributors that are worth adding to your holiday shopping list (and your bookshelf).

items.title: The Summit of Self-Promotion
items.desc: Despite claiming that world history was made in Shenzhen with the US–Russia–China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace, the trilateral summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin was about optics, not substance. One of the many important problems they failed to address was China’s export-led growth.

items.title: Why Nvidia Couldn’t Quit Jensen Huang
items.desc: Developing AI requires tremendous coordination across firms and sectors, from the AI labs themselves to energy and computing infrastructure, as well as long-term vision and patience. Whereas much of this coordination and planning is led by the government in China, in the US, it has been driven largely by one CEO.

items.title: Chips Too Big to Fail
items.desc: The Trump administration pushed for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as CEO of Nvidia to keep the stock market high, to feed a possible productivity surge, and to advance a US foreign policy built on reconciliation with China. But will Americans continue to believe in the AI miracle and this new version of Chimerica?

items.title: Amplifying the Voice of Human Limits
items.desc: Tech leaders like Elon Musk have embraced Prometheus as a symbol of creation, conquest, and discovery. But the Promethean impulse must be balanced by the “Orphic” tradition’s respect for and contemplation of nature’s mystery.

items.title: Making the Most of South Korea’s Semiconductor Boom
items.desc: The AI boom has driven South Korea’s economic growth well above expectations, thanks to soaring demand for advanced semiconductors. But AI’s transformative potential does not guarantee that the current investment frenzy will continue, leaving the economy vulnerable to a downturn.

items.title: Is a Financial-Market Reckoning Imminent?
items.desc: After a year of unprecedented AI investment, increasingly financed by debt in opaque private markets, growing unease about the industry’s future is reflected in sharp declines in the NASDAQ index and the S&P 500. But the stock market’s dependence on a handful of highly leveraged companies—and even a single CEO—is hardly the only source of global financial risk. Amid mounting fears, we asked PS contributors what to expect from financial markets in the year ahead.

items.title: The African Union’s Elusive Quest for Security
items.desc: The African Union has long sought to implement Ali Mazrui’s concept of Pax Africana, but has faced persistent logistical and financial constraints. The key to making peacekeeping operations more effective is establishing a better division of labor between the AU, the United Nations, and regional African organizations.

items.title: The Achilles’ Heel of Emerging Economies’ Trade
items.desc: New research shows that 23% of global goods imports in 2024 faced at least two of three vulnerabilities: product criticality, supply concentration, and geopolitical distance. Given the wide range of problems, early diagnosis and targeted action are particularly important for emerging economies with limited fiscal space.

items.title: AI Agents Could Make Big Tech Bigger
items.desc: The rise of agentic AI could give a handful of Big Tech firms unprecedented power over our personal lives. Unless lawmakers and regulators act now, these digital gatekeepers could manipulate consumers, turbocharge corporate surveillance, and threaten our individual rights and civil liberties.

items.title: If the AI Bubble Is Bursting, the Fallout Will Be Severe
items.desc: With the S&P 500 following the tech-heavy NASDAQ into correction territory, even as Anthropic set a record with its initial public offering, this is a good moment to compare AI stock valuations with earlier asset-price bubbles. A look back at the dot-com boom and bust of the late 1990s offers ample cause for concern.

items.title: Journalism Can Be More Than AI Fodder
items.desc: As AI fundamentally alters the information environment, news publishers risk becoming little more than content suppliers for Big Tech. To avoid that fate, many are drawing on their archives and expertise to develop AI tools that allow them to operate and compete on their own terms.

items.title: Governing African Economies as They Are
items.desc: Africa cannot overcome its development challenges by applying the same knowledge, economic, and innovation systems that helped create them. Imagining and governing new ways forward will require three intellectual ruptures.

items.title: Making Earth Cool Again
items.desc: Climate multilateralism is evolving into a two-tiered system in which high-level negotiations toward shared commitments and the real-world implementation of climate solutions become more mutually supportive. Only by unleashing such virtuous cycles can we keep the 1.5ºC target for global warming within reach.

items.title: America’s Lame-Duck Autocrat
items.desc: When autocrats suffer a defeat, they tend to double down, such as by intensifying repression at home or behaving more recklessly abroad. With two years left in office after historic midterm election losses, this is the road US President Donald Trump appears to be taking.

Whereas the old conservatism was based on Christian faith, libertarian economics, and flag-waving patriotism, the alt-right saw America as a white racial nation-state, rejected the idea of free markets, and was basically irreligious and isolationist. items.desc: Five high-quality surveys ask about AI in different ways. Their wording matters, but the overall picture is consistent.

items.desc: What is someone’s risk of developing depression, anxiety, or other mental health issues at some point in their life?

items.desc: Around one-fifth of development aid is spent on climate-related projects. But what does climate-related mean, and does it crowd out other aid projects?

items.desc: We use long-run census data to understand the scale of recent US migration trends, and how these compare to previous centuries.

items.desc: Organic farming often wins when we compare impacts on one unit of land, but there is no clear winner when we look at impacts per unit of food production.

items.title: A never-ending childhood of malaria
items.desc: How often do people in high-burden areas get malaria? Studies suggest that many children can experience five or more malaria infections a year.

items.title: Beef production in Brazil has been the largest driver of global deforestation in recent decades
items.desc: Most beef production in Brazil is to meet domestic rather than international demand.

items.title: Judge the Cyber Apocalypse by the Data, Not the Headlines
items.desc: The technical metrics on AI for cybersecurity now indicate that recent advances are enabling attackers more than defenders and that AI is regularly being used in attacks. This is in line with daily news stories on the “vulnpocalypse” and “Black October.” Surprisingly though, data on real-world impacts of cyber attacks tells a less dire story. If this trend continues, it could indicate that attribution and punishment matter at least as much as attackers’ technical capabilities. items.desc: CSET’s Sam Bresnick and Emelia Probasco shared their expert analysis in an op-ed published by Lawfare. items.title: Biodata Matters for the Genesis Mission
items.desc: The Genesis Mission aims to harness artificial intelligence to supercharge scientific innovation and support the United States’ technological leadership, including in biotechnology. Accomplishing this goal requires lots of diverse, high-quality biological data, and the Mission plans to pull together federal datasets accordingly. This piece describes the categories of biodata challenges that the Genesis Mission is likely to face and makes recommendations about how to approach them. During the interview, Feldgoise also shared his insights on Nvidia’s earnings and other developments in the semiconductor industry. items.title: Dutch resist ‘unacceptable’ US bid to tighten semiconductor export controls
items.desc: CSET's Hanna Dohmen was featured in an article published by POLITICO Europe examining the Netherlands' opposition to proposed U.S. restrictions on semiconductor exports to China. The article discusses how the proposed MATCH Act could affect Dutch chipmaking equipment manufacturer ASML and create tensions between the United States and its European allies. items.title: Convergent Interests: How America Could Undermine Its Own AI Advantage
items.desc: A convergence of political, commercial, and ideological pressures can impede America’s AI leadership, and public controversies are powerful enough to catalyze that convergence. Our piece spotlights this issue, urging policymakers to govern AI responsibly without disabling the innovation that makes American leadership possible—even in the wake of scandal. The post Convergent Interests: How America Could Undermine Its Own AI Advantage appeared first on Center for Security and Emerging Technology .
